title: Monte Carlo Poker Equity Simulator
summary: My MITES Semester project uses repeated deals to estimate Texas Hold’em equity from known cards.
question: How much of the pot is a hand worth when some of the cards are still unknown?

figure.alt: Estimated preflop equity is 85% for pocket aces, 67% for ace-king suited, and 34% for seven-two offsuit against one random opponent.
figure.caption: An example run of my Python simulator. Each hand was tested over 8,000 seeded deals against one random opponent, with split pots counted toward equity.

symbol.name: omega
symbol.meaning: the set of every way the unseen cards could fall.

sections.title: What I built
sections.text: I started from an example C++ program and wrote the simulator in Python. It samples unseen cards, finds each player’s best five-card hand, and compares the ranks with exact tie-break rules. A fixed random seed lets a scenario be rerun. I separated the Python simulation from the Streamlit interface. I presented it at the MITES symposium.

sections.title: What I learned
sections.text: Equity includes the share of the pot you take when a hand ties. Making that distinction meant testing split pots as well as edge cases in hand ranking, from ace-low straights to kicker ties.
